title: Geopolitics: a Russian supermajority, a US-China AI channel and migration's hard edges
summary: Russia's ruling party kept a supermajority and the question is how the Kremlin uses it, while Washington and Beijing opened an AI-safety channel ahead of a Trump-Xi summit. Migration dominated a second cluster: migrants stranded in Ceuta, US deportation deals and abuse allegations in Equatorial Guinea, and a solidarity-shirt row in Spanish football. Elsewhere, the UN called US strikes on alleged drug boats potential crimes against humanity, Typhoon Dujuan forced evacuations in Japan, and US networks boycotted a White House event as a lawsuit and a low approval rating landed. Geo drew on wire coverage only — GDELT, ISW and Polymarket were unavailable — so sourcing is broad-outlet rather than specialist.

stories.headline: Putin’s party wins supermajority in Russia’s parliamentary election
stories.dek: The Kremlin's party kept its dominance as voting concluded, and analysts are watching how the result is used rather than the count itself.
tldr: Al Jazeera reported that Putin's party won a supermajority in Russia's parliamentary election, held amid ramped-up Ukrainian attacks.
The BBC said the elections produced few surprises and that how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial.
DW reported separately that Ukraine is stepping up measures to protect its railways.

body.text: Al Jazeera reported that President Vladimir Putin's party won a supermajority in Russia's parliamentary election, a result it placed against ramped-up Ukrainian attacks during the voting period.
The BBC described Russia's elections as having produced few surprises, adding that how the Kremlin uses the results will be the crucial part.
Separately, DW reported that Ukraine is stepping up measures to protect its railways.

stories.whyItMatters: A supermajority gives the Kremlin a freer domestic hand while wartime logistics — including Ukraine's rail network — stay in the crosshairs, so the vote's consequences are as much about wartime resilience as about party politics.
stories.editorNote: The supermajority description comes from Al Jazeera and the BBC; DW's rail item is a separate report cited for context. No independent vote tally was reviewed.

stories.headline: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
stories.dek: AI safety is being folded into a wider trade and technology contest, with Europe squeezed between the two economies.
tldr: The BBC reported that the US and China discussed an AI safety plan ahead of a Trump-Xi summit.
DW described the broader US-China rivalry as reshaping global trade and leaving Europe caught in the middle.
The Guardian reported why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development.

body.text: The BBC reported that the US and China discussed an AI safety plan ahead of a Trump-Xi summit.
DW described the wider US-China rivalry as reshaping global trade, with Europe caught in the middle.
The Guardian reported why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development.

stories.whyItMatters: AI safety is being folded into a broader trade and technology contest, so any joint plan is also a signal about how far the two economies will coordinate on chips, models and standards — and how much room that leaves for Europe.
stories.editorNote: All three items are wire reports; no joint statement text was reviewed, so the scope of any safety plan remains unconfirmed.

stories.headline: How thousands of migrants stranded in Ceuta are surviving
stories.dek: Ceuta's stranded migrants, US deportation deals and abuse allegations in Equatorial Guinea point at the same hard edge of enforcement.
tldr: Al Jazeera reported on how thousands of migrants stranded in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta are surviving.
The Guardian published an investigation into what it called Trump's secret deportation deals, and separately reported abuse allegations involving men deported to Equatorial Guinea.
Al Jazeera reported that the Ceuta crisis spilled into Spanish football in a solidarity-shirt row.

body.text: Al Jazeera reported on how thousands of migrants stranded in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta are surviving.

The Guardian published an investigation it headlined 'Banished to alien lands', describing Trump's secret deportation deals, and separately reported that lawyers say men deported from the US were bound and beaten in an Equatorial Guinea detention hotel.
Al Jazeera reported that the Ceuta crisis spilled into Spanish football in a solidarity-shirt row.

stories.whyItMatters: Migration enforcement is increasingly outsourced and contested, and the Ceuta and deportation threads show the same pressure point — how states move and hold people outside their own legal systems — from two different directions.
stories.editorNote: Deportation accounts are attributed to lawyers via The Guardian and were not independently verified; Ceuta conditions come from Al Jazeera's own reporting.

The Guardian reported that a UN expert said the strikes may constitute 'crimes against humanity'.
Both items report the same UN assessment through different outlets.
